title: What You See From the Right

concept.title: The last node of every level
body: Stand on the right side of a tree and look at it: on each level you see the **rightmost node**, because it hides the others on the same level. So the answer is the last node of every level. A level-order walk that processes one level at a time gives it directly: after taking the nodes of a level, the last one taken is the rightmost.

body.code:
view = []
level = [root]
while level:
    view.append(level[-1].val)               # the rightmost node of this level
    level = [child for node in level for child in (node.left, node.right) if child is not None]
print(*view)

body: A node on a deeper level can still be seen when the right side of the tree is shorter: the left subtree can have a deeper level that is visible because the right side has no node there. The level-by-level walk handles this automatically.

statement: Imagine standing on the right side of a binary tree. Print the values of the nodes that you see, from the top level to the bottom level: on every level the rightmost node. Print them on one line separated by spaces.
inputFormat: The first line has `t`, the number of words in the description of the tree.
The second line has the tree in level order: the root first, then the children of the nodes row by row from left to right. `N` stands for a missing child. There is no `N` at the end.
constraints: The height of the tree is at most 800.

examples.note: The rightmost nodes of the levels are 1, 3 and 4.
The deepest level has only the node 4, which is visible from the right.

hints: Go through the tree level by level.
The last node of each level is the one that is visible.
Keep the nodes of the current level in a list and build the next level from their children.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


# Builds a binary tree from a level-order list of words; "N" marks a missing child.
def build_tree(vals):
    if not vals or vals[0] == "N":
        return None
    root = TreeNode(int(vals[0]))
    queue = [root]
    head = 0
    i = 1
    while head < len(queue) and i < len(vals):
        node = queue[head]
        head += 1
        if vals[i] != "N":
            node.left = TreeNode(int(vals[i]))
            queue.append(node.left)
        i += 1
        if i < len(vals) and vals[i] != "N":
            node.right = TreeNode(int(vals[i]))
            queue.append(node.right)
        i += 1
    return root


# Prints a tree in the same level-order form ("empty" for no tree).
def print_tree(root):
    if root is None:
        print("empty")
        return
    out = []
    queue = [root]
    head = 0
    while head < len(queue):
        node = queue[head]
        head += 1
        if node is None:
            out.append("N")
        else:
            out.append(str(node.val))
            queue.append(node.left)
            queue.append(node.right)
    while out and out[-1] == "N":
        out.pop()
    print(" ".join(out))

explanation: The tree is processed one level at a time; the last node of each level is recorded, and the next level is made of the children of the nodes of this level.
